title: An EHR is an ecosystem, not a single screen
overview: Explore how an electronic health record brings longitudinal information together across settings and authorized users. Trace information from departmental source systems through standardization and exchange to use in a workflow, and consider how interoperability, governance, and HIM responsibilities support meaningful and trustworthy information.
objectives: Explain that an EHR supports longitudinal information across settings and authorized users.
Describe interoperability as technical connection, shared meaning, and usable workflow.
Explain how an EHR depends on multiple source systems.
Use the Source → Standardize → Exchange → Use framework to explain information flow, responsibility, and points of control.
Distinguish an EMR from an EHR by their scope and focus.
Describe HIM responsibilities for protecting information meaning, quality, trust, and use in EHR-related work.

concepts.definition: Principles addressing purpose and fit; data and meaning; access and trust; and workflow and adoption, supported by controls such as scope, workflow fit, measurable objectives, definitions, metadata, validation, mapping, policy, role-based access, authentication, logs, user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities in EHR-related work
concepts.definition: Explain system purpose; support definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; check identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency; support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

concepts.name: Source → Standardize → Exchange → Use
concepts.definition: A sequence for capturing data in departmental and clinical systems, mapping concepts and formats to shared standards, transmitting authorized information between systems, and presenting information in a workflow where a person can act.

sections.body: An electronic health record (EHR) supports longitudinal information across settings and authorized users. It is designed for continuity and authorized exchange, rather than being limited to documentation within one provider or organization. The EHR depends on information from multiple source systems, including registration, laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, and documentation systems. Thinking of the EHR as an ecosystem emphasizes the connected information and work behind the record, not just the screen on which information appears.
sections.title: An EHR is broader than a single screen

sections.body: Interoperability has three connected requirements: systems must connect technically, exchanged information must have shared meaning, and the information must be presented in a usable workflow where a person can act. A connection alone does not ensure that information is understandable or useful. Clinical vocabularies make concepts computable and comparable; HL7 and FHIR are identified as supporting structured exchange patterns. In the laboratory example, a standard exchange format carries a result while a clinical vocabulary gives the test and unit consistent meaning. The information becomes useful in practice when it is presented within a workflow where a person can act.
sections.title: Interoperability requires connection, meaning, and workflow

sections.body: Use Source → Standardize → Exchange → Use to follow information and identify where responsibility and control matter. Source means capturing data in departmental and clinical systems. Standardize means mapping concepts and formats to shared standards. Exchange means transmitting authorized information between systems. Use means presenting the information in a workflow where a person can act. For a laboratory result entering the EHR, the laboratory system is the source; a standard format and vocabulary support standardization; the result is transmitted to the EHR; and the workflow must present it for use. The sequence links technical movement to meaning and work.
sections.title: Trace information through the four-step framework

sections.body: An electronic medical record (EMR) is an electronic record within one provider or organization, focused on local clinical documentation. An EHR is broader: it is a longitudinal record designed for authorized exchange and continuity across multiple settings. The distinction is one of scope and focus. A local clinical documentation record fits the EMR description; a record designed to support authorized information exchange across settings fits the EHR description.
sections.title: Distinguish EMR from EHR

sections.body: Reliable EHR information depends on purpose and fit; data and meaning; access and trust; and workflow and adoption. Controls include scope, workflow fit, and measurable objectives; definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping; policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs; and user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement. Audit logs, signatures, and copy-forward controls also support trust and accountability. HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work: explain users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits; protect meaning through definitions and consistent interpretation; check identity and information quality; support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.
sections.title: Governance and HIM responsibilities

activities.title: Follow a laboratory result
activities.prompt: A laboratory result enters an EHR from a departmental laboratory system. A standard exchange format carries it, and a clinical vocabulary gives the test and unit consistent meaning. Which interpretation best explains what is needed for interoperability to be useful?
activities.debrief: Interoperability includes technical connection, shared meaning, and usable workflow. In the example, the exchange format carries the result, the vocabulary gives the test and unit consistent meaning, and workflow presentation makes the information usable.

The result should remain only in the departmental system because an EHR does not depend on source systems.
A clinical vocabulary replaces the need to transmit authorized information between systems.
